One-sentence judgment: captains, mates, and pilots of water vessels are not about "taking the boat out"; they carry final safety and compliance responsibility for a voyage or a docking and undocking while weather, depth, currents, visibility, and vessel condition keep changing: preparing and executing the passage plan, giving and repeating orders, cross-monitoring, checking against checklists, and stopping the voyage or refusing unsafe operations and escalating when uncertain. O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), does not mark it Bright Outlook, and gives an interest code of RCE (Realistic, Conventional, Enterprising). The core boundary: in the United States a license issued by the U.S. Coast Guard is generally required, while in mainland China captains and mates must obtain the corresponding certificates of competency as required and pilots must be employed by a pilotage institution and hold certificates of competency limited by category, grade, and scope; a pilot's professional advice does not relieve the captain and bridge watchkeeping personnel of their safety duties.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to write out the passage plan, tides and weather, depths and hazards, and abort conditions before departure and to check them item by item against the checklist; you can maintain situational awareness when multiple instruments, radio, and visual information change at once (the O*NET work context shows 88% have face-to-face discussions every day and 76% consider the impact of decisions on colleagues or company results very important); you are willing to give orders in standard phraseology and require read-back and can accept continuous monitoring and cross-checking; and you accept a daily routine centered on voyage records, watch and rest records, and compliance reports.

Conditions for pausing major investment first: you have not yet completed one full closed loop from the passage plan and master-pilot exchange through the docking and undocking manoeuvring sequence to abort conditions and emergency escalation; or you are unwilling to record watch and rest hours as required and unwilling to stop the voyage or refuse instructions when uncertain; also, do not treat recreational inland or lake boating experience as proof that you can independently handle harbour pilotage or command of a large vessel.

Education, credentials, and authorization must be checked separately: O*NET classifies this occupation as Job Zone Three (medium preparation, SVP 6.0 to below 7.0); it usually requires vocational school training, related on-the-job experience, or an associate degree (the O*NET education survey shows 42% of respondents consider a high school diploma or equivalent sufficient, 37% consider a postsecondary certificate necessary, and 8% consider a bachelor's degree necessary), plus one to two years of on-the-job training (the O*NET occupation page lists 2 apprenticeship directions: Officer in Charge of Navigational Watch and Pilot, Ship). Statutory qualifications are the key threshold for this occupation: the United States requires a license issued by the U.S. Coast Guard (the O*NET certification page lists several officer and route certificates issued by the U.S. Coast Guard National Maritime Center, such as National Master 500/1600 OC or NC and STCW II/2 - OSV Master 3000 GT Or More Management Level); in mainland China, under the Crew Regulations of the People's Republic of China and the rules for the examination and issuance of certificates of competency for seafarers, captains and mates must complete crew registration, health, basic safety and the corresponding competency training, service history, and examinations, with certificates limited by navigation area, capacity, and vessel grade; pilots additionally must be employed by a pilotage institution under the pilot management measures and hold certificates of competency limited by harbour or inland category, grade, and pilotage scope. A certificate itself does not automatically bring owner employment, authorization for a specific vessel, or external signing authority, and a pilot's professional duties do not relieve the captain and bridge watchkeeping personnel of their safety duties.

In one sentence: this is a role that turns "can the vessel safely complete this leg as planned" into reviewable evidence; the outputs are the passage plan and master-pilot exchange records, bridge orders and read-back records, watch and rest records, vessel and equipment inspection records, and pollution prevention and compliance reports; it is not the role that approves the owner's business decisions or vessel design, nor does it replace the competent authority's regulation of transport vehicles, licenses, and competency. This page does not publish occupation-level wage figures for mainland China and only registers the scope and gaps with visible markers.

The work of this occupation falls into three categories: first, navigation and manoeuvring (preparing and executing the passage plan, directing course and speed based on weather, depth, currents, and hazards, docking and undocking and narrow-water manoeuvring, and using aids such as radar, echo sounders, radio, lights, and buoys); second, watchkeeping and monitoring (standing navigational watches at specified periods, continuously monitoring instruments and sea state and other vessels' movements, checking against checklists, orders with read-back and cross-monitoring, and reporting and escalating abnormalities as needed); third, management and compliance (managing crew, watches, and cabin allocation, supervising loading and discharge and cargo and passenger condition, maintaining equipment and life-saving and firefighting appliances, organizing safety drills, and recording voyage, weather, pollution control, and compliance information). All three share the same chain built around the passage plan, order read-back, and reviewable records.
Navigation and manoeuvring

Receive the voyage task and vessel, cargo, and passenger information → consult charts, tides, weather, and notices to mariners → prepare the passage plan and set abort conditions → monitor on watch and cross-check radar and visual information → manoeuvre with standard orders and read-back confirmation → record position, movements, and weather
Watchkeeping and monitoring

Editorial process: hand over and check position, course, and equipment → monitor continuously and cross-check → identify abnormalities and notify the responsible person immediately → handle safely according to the situation → record the event and hand over; this is not authorization to operate a specific vessel.

Complete the master-pilot exchange before docking or undocking or narrow-water manoeuvring → confirm tugs, lines, anchors, thrusters, and communications are ready → execute the manoeuvres in sequence with read-back on key actions → check berthing position, line tension, and vessel attitude → record the manoeuvring process, deviations, and disposition → complete the compliance report and handover

Captains, mates, and pilots of water vessels have as their core output navigational safety, compliance, and reviewable records; marine engineers and naval architects handle the design and maintenance of hull, power, and systems; fishing and hunting workers engage in fishing and hunting work; commercial divers perform underwater work; riggers perform lifting and lashing work; aircraft cargo handling supervisors organize air cargo loading; sailors and marine oilers carry out deck, engine room, and watch duties. Similar names or being in the same transport and operations chain do not mean that navigational command authority, statutory licenses, vessel manoeuvring authorization, and external signing authority are interchangeable.
Core purpose

Get the vessel safely to its destination and complete operations as planned under the given hydrographic, meteorological, and traffic conditions: control risk through the passage plan and abort conditions, ensure orders are executed accurately through read-back and cross-monitoring, and make the process reviewable through records and reports.
Main objects and basis

The objects are water transport vehicles such as vessels, tugs, and ferries, propulsion, steering, thrusters, anchors, lines, and towing equipment, radar, echo sounders, electronic charts, radio, and navigational aids, charts, tide tables, weather, and notices to mariners, cargo, passenger, ballast, and pollution prevention related systems, life-saving and firefighting equipment, and watch, rest, and compliance records; the basis is international and domestic navigation safety and collision avoidance rules, licenses and certificates of competency and navigation area limitations issued by the competent authority, the vessel's safety management system and checklists, port and pilotage rules, hours of work and rest regulations, and the related requirements for crew competency and vessel manning.
Core process

Receiving the task and materials, preparing the passage plan, checking hydrographic, meteorological, and notice information, watchkeeping and monitoring, orders with read-back manoeuvring, docking and undocking and narrow-water operations, abnormality identification and escalation, recording and reporting, and watch handover.
Main outputs

The passage plan and abort conditions, master-pilot exchange records, bridge orders and read-back and cross-monitoring records, watch and rest records, vessel and equipment inspection and maintenance records, docking and undocking manoeuvring records, cargo, passenger, and pollution prevention related records, and compliance reports and handover records.
Accountable party

The captain carries navigational command and management responsibility, while deck officers such as the chief mate and pilots act according to their actual duties, and the owner must also ensure safe conditions and manning. Article 31 of China's Maritime Traffic Safety Law: pilotage does not relieve the captain of command and management responsibility; Article 34 prohibits sailing recklessly and the owner may not compel it; Article 38 allows the captain to decide independently on life safety, security, and pollution prevention. 
When an abnormality occurs, notify the bridge watchkeeping officer in charge or the captain immediately, and the person with the corresponding duties takes safe measures based on the actual navigational situation; slowing down, stopping, handing over, or refusing the operation are each assessed separately, and stopping the voyage first cannot be applied uniformly. The captain makes safety decisions independently under the law, and internal requests for instructions do not replace this.
Authority and approval

Seagoing deck officer competency in China is checked against the 2026 amended rules by navigation area, capacity, grade, vessel, and function; health, basic safety, competency/special training, service history, and examinations are checked per task, and the watchkeeping certificate is valid for no more than 5 years and until the 66th birthday. Pilotage additionally requires obtaining the corresponding harbour/inland category, grade, and scope certificate under the 2025 measures and being employed by a pilotage institution; the seagoing rules do not cover the complete inland licensing requirements. 
Article 31 of China's Maritime Traffic Safety Law: pilotage does not relieve the captain of command and management responsibility; Article 34 prohibits sailing recklessly and the owner may not compel it; Article 38 allows the captain to decide independently on life safety, security, and pollution prevention. 
Article 26 of China's pilotage provisions requires both parties to exchange the pilotage plan and vessel manoeuvring information; Article 33 is a principle of cooperation and adoption, with an exception when safety is endangered, allowing a request to change the order, to ask the institution to replace the pilot when necessary, and to report to the maritime authority promptly. Article 30 requires the pilot to inform the captain and properly arrange for the vessel's safety before refusing, suspending, or terminating; the vessel is not simply abandoned or stopped suddenly.
Conclusion boundaries

Voyage and watch records state "what happened under the given vessel, personnel, hydrographic, meteorological, and traffic conditions"; they do not equal exemption from responsibility, nor do they replace the competent authority's determination of an accident or violation, and they are updated as navigation data, watch and rest records, and notices to mariners change; when citing them, state the vessel, navigation area, certificate scope, and record period as well.

Before starting, check at least six items: job duties (harbour pilotage, inland or coastal watchkeeping, towing and ferry service, or engineering and special operations vessels), the category, grade, and navigation area limitations of the license or certificate of competency held, vessel manning and watch and rest arrangements, the qualifications and safety management system of the owner or organization, whether specific vessel type, cargo, or passenger operation qualifications are needed, and whether you are responsible for external reports and signing.
Occupation scope

Occupation identity O*NET-SOC53-5021.00; ZoneThree, not marked Bright Outlook. Interest RCE: R77/C59/E54/I27/S15/A0; the specific-field scores of transportation/machine operation 88, management/administration 60, and nature/outdoors 43 are counted separately and are not R sub-scores or a personal admission line. 
O*NET2025 industry distribution: transportation and warehousing 71%, other 29% (including government); this is the occupation classification distribution, not wages or a Chinese industry mapping. Seagoing deck officer work, inland navigation, and pilotage in China must be checked against the actual duties and their respective certificate systems, and no one-to-one wage mapping has been established.
Education and training paths

The O*NET entry-level education survey shows 42% high school/equivalent, 37% postsecondary certificate, and 8% bachelor's degree; the categories shown are not the complete distribution and are not incumbent education. For this occupation the BLS gives typical entry-level education postsecondary non-degree certificate, related experience less than 5 years, and OJT None; the broad Zone Three training of one to two years is not a deadline for all positions. The apprenticeship examples Officer in Charge of Navig Watch and Pilot, Ship are not current enrollment or a uniform requirement. In China, seagoing deck officer competency is checked against the 2026 amended rules by navigation area, capacity, grade, vessel, and function; health, basic safety, competency/special training, service history, and examinations are checked per task, and the watchkeeping certificate is valid for no more than 5 years and until the 66th birthday. Pilotage additionally requires obtaining the corresponding harbour/inland category, grade, and scope certificate under the 2025 measures and being employed by a pilotage institution; the seagoing rules do not cover the complete inland licensing requirements.
Methods and tools

13 software categories, 7 hot products, 1 InDemand (Office); U.S. postings for all of 2025 at Office5%, Excel2%, Outlook1%, with macOS/Revit/PowerPoint/Word as NA not 0; a posting mention does not equal deployment, efficiency, automation rate, or a mandatory threshold. 
On-board tools include radar, electronic charts, echo sounders, radio, navigational aids, and steering and line handling equipment, checked against the actual vessel configuration.
Safety and work permits

The work is mainly shipboard shifts and bridge watches, possibly away from home for weeks or months at a time; pilots board and leave vessels more often at a specific port or route segment. The main demands come from weather, night navigation, narrow waters, noise, and continuous monitoring, plus the living arrangements of long absences from home, and watch arrangements must control fatigue. The O*NET work context shows: 88% have face-to-face discussions every day; 82% work more than 40 hours per week; 72% are exposed daily to distracting or uncomfortable noise; 72% consider the consequences of errors extremely serious; 73% have extremely high responsibility for the health and safety of others; 69% are in an enclosed vehicle or operating enclosed equipment every day; 66% wear common protective or safety equipment every day; 62% are exposed to various weather conditions outdoors every day; 61% use their hands continuously or almost continuously to operate, control, or perceive objects and tools; 51% are exposed to contaminants every day; 49% are exposed to whole body vibration every day; 47% face time pressure every day. Operations must follow the safety management system and checklists, implement watch and rest rules, and protect line handling and boarding and leaving operations per procedures; when an abnormality occurs, notify the bridge watchkeeping officer in charge or the captain immediately, and the person with the corresponding duties takes safe measures based on the actual navigational situation; slowing down, stopping, handing over, or refusing the operation are each assessed separately, and stopping the voyage first cannot be applied uniformly. The captain makes safety decisions independently under the law, and internal requests for instructions do not replace this.
Training and regulatory requirements

Seagoing deck officer competency in China is checked against the 2026 amended rules by navigation area, capacity, grade, vessel, and function; health, basic safety, competency/special training, service history, and examinations are checked per task, and the watchkeeping certificate is valid for no more than 5 years and until the 66th birthday. Pilotage additionally requires obtaining the corresponding harbour/inland category, grade, and scope certificate under the 2025 measures and being employed by a pilotage institution; the seagoing rules do not cover the complete inland licensing requirements. 
In the United States, 46 CFR 15.401 requires checking TWIC and/or MMC, the corresponding endorsement, medical, and any required STCW according to the capacity served; pilotage in some states also requires a state license, and a directory link does not replace the statutory conditions.
Pay and hours

O*NET82% typically work more than 40 hours per week, and 47% face strict deadlines daily; schedules are 46% regular / 42% irregular / 12% seasonal, and some deep-sea or barge voyages involve long absences from home, which does not represent every position. In 2025 the U.S. median was 92460 USD/year and 44.45/hour; U.S. SOC53-5021 for this occupation: about 41300 in 2025 → 42900 projected in 2035, a change of 4.0% (average), a BLS net change of about 1700, and an average of 3800 openings per year over 2025—2035, which is not net growth; the rounded employment endpoints are not used to back-calculate the net change. Exact national wages for this occupation in China are still insufficient evidence; the NBS2025 figure for transportation, warehousing, and postal services non-private 133981 / private 73133 yuan pre-tax annual average is a multi-occupation industry background related to shipping business, and is not captain, mate, or pilot pay, starting pay, monthly pay, or an individual quote. 
When comparing opportunities, check the certificate, vessel type, voyage, actual schedule, and pay composition separately.

Captains, mates, and pilots of water vessels (O*NET-SOC 53-5021.00) command or supervise the operation of ships and water vessels, such as tugboats and ferryboats, and in the United States are generally required to hold a license issued by the U.S. Coast Guard. Daily work includes: directing the course and speed of vessels based on expert knowledge of local wind, weather, depth, tides, currents, and hazards; preventing vessels under navigational control from engaging in unsafe operations; acting as the docking commander when a vessel arrives at a port or berth; consulting charts, tables, weather reports, or navigational equipment to determine and direct vessel movements; manoeuvring vessels using radio, echo sounders, radar, lights, buoys, or lighthouses; operating ship-to-shore radio to exchange information needed for vessel operations; docking and undocking and possibly manoeuvring in narrow spaces such as locks; standing navigational watches at specified periods; inspecting vessels and equipment to ensure efficient and safe operation and regulatory compliance; reading gauges to confirm hydraulic oil, air pressure, or oxygen levels; reporting violations of federal or state pilotage regulations to the competent authority; assisting in maritime rescue; signalling passing vessels with whistles, flashing lights, semaphore, or radio; measuring water depth; signalling crew or deckhands to tie or cast off towlines, open or close gates or ramps, or rig guard rails; maintaining on-board engines, winches, navigation systems, fire extinguishers, or life-saving equipment; recording daily activities, personnel reports, vessel position and movement, ports of call, weather and sea state, pollution control work, and cargo or passenger status; advising the captain on port rules and customs procedures; supervising the loading or unloading of cargo or equipment for compliance with standards; using electronic sounding equipment and calculating landmark fixes against chart depth contours; learning new systems and procedures through instruction, simulators, or models; directing or coordinating operations such as loading and unloading, steering, engine room, and equipment repair; arranging fueling, resupply, or repairs; supervising the cleaning and maintenance of decks, superstructures, and the bridge; purchasing supplies and equipment; towing and manoeuvring barges or commanding tugboats; inspecting port areas or shorelines for oil spills or other contaminants; assigning watches and living quarters; interviewing and hiring crew; conducting safety drills such as man overboard or fire; and supervising drones for inspection and maintenance of hard-to-reach parts of the vessel. It carries navigational safety, compliance, and recording responsibility, but does not replace the owner's business decisions, nor the competent authority's regulation of vessels, licenses, and competency.

paragraphs: This page compares captains, mates, and pilots of water vessels with six adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which direction each preference is better suited to. Adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupation descriptions and do not mean the job titles or licenses are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career direction and core outputs are based on O*NET-SOC 53-5021.00 and the official descriptions of the adjacent entries (U.S. scope); the adjacent occupations listed by this evidence route are marine engineers and naval architects, fishing and hunting workers, commercial divers, riggers, and aircraft cargo handling supervisors, with sailors and marine oilers being O*NET related occupations; navigational command authority, statutory licenses and certificates of competency, vessel manoeuvring authorization, and external signing confirmation authority must be verified separately for each company and jurisdiction, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut for changing careers.

The table below compares the differences in duties and outputs between captains, mates, and pilots of water vessels and the adjacent directions; the basis for judging is the main outputs, what the work is accountable for, and the required authorization, not how similar the job titles are.

Marine engineers and naval architects deal with the design and technical condition of hulls and propulsion systems, usually working in a shore-based or shipyard environment; this occupation deals with real-time navigation and manoeuvring and must get it right in one attempt under non-repeatable hydrographic, meteorological, and traffic conditions.

If you would rather do the design and maintenance of vessels and systems, look first at the marine engineer and naval architect direction; if you would rather carry navigational command and watchkeeping responsibility on the bridge, look first at this occupation.
Take on the design and maintenance of hull, propulsion, and mechanical systems, with output mainly design documents and equipment maintenance records.
Marine Engineers and Naval Architects

Fishing and hunting workers work mainly on fishing operations and fishing gear handling, with the pace constrained by fishing seasons and permits; this occupation is accountable for the navigational safety and compliance of transport vessels and is bound by collision avoidance rules and the license and competency system.

If you would rather engage in fishing and gear work, look first at the fishing and hunting worker direction; if you would rather take on vessel navigational command and safety management, look first at this occupation.
Engage in fishing and hunting operations, with output mainly catches and operation records.
Fishing and Hunting Workers

entries.answer: Command or supervise the operation of ships and water vessels; direct course and speed based on expert knowledge of local wind, weather, depth, tides, currents, and hazards; prevent vessels under navigational control from engaging in unsafe operations; act as docking commander when arriving at a port or berth; consult charts, tables, weather reports, or navigational equipment to determine and direct vessel movements; manoeuvre vessels using radio, echo sounders, radar, lights, buoys, or lighthouses; operate ship-to-shore radio to exchange operational information; dock and undock and possibly manoeuvre in narrow spaces such as locks; stand navigational watches at specified periods; inspect vessels and equipment to ensure safe operation and regulatory compliance; read gauges to confirm hydraulic oil and air pressure or oxygen levels; report violations of pilotage regulations to the competent authority; assist in maritime rescue; maintain on-board engines, winches, navigation, firefighting, and life-saving equipment; record daily activities, vessel position, ports of call, weather, pollution control, and cargo or passenger status; supervise loading and unloading and cargo and passenger condition; arrange fueling, resupply, and repairs; and assign watches and cabins and conduct safety drills.
entries.question: What do captains, mates, and pilots of water vessels do every day?

entries.answer: The main risks are grounding from misjudging depth or currents, manoeuvring conflicts from omitted bridge information exchange or orders without read-back, reduced attention from continuous watches and fatigue, pilot boarding and leaving injuries in rough sea states, over-trusting automatic alarms, and working beyond the license or competency scope and mishandling pollution prevention; control depends on the passage plan and abort conditions, the master-pilot exchange, standard orders with read-back and cross-monitoring, watch and rest records, checking raw information against the checklist, and stopping the voyage or refusing unsafe operations and emergency escalation.
entries.question: What risks does this job most require you to watch out for in advance?

entries.answer: Fit signals are maintaining situational awareness when multiple instruments, radio, and visual information change at once, being willing to cross-check against the checklist, and being able to give clear orders and read-back under pressure and escalate uncertainty promptly; what matters is whether there are reviewable passage plans, master-pilot exchange records, watch and rest records, and compliance performance, not just an interest in navigation.
entries.question: How do you judge whether this job suits you?

entries.answer: Route checking and chart information retrieval, sensor alarm consolidation, draft records and reports, and equipment condition prediction can be assisted; passage plan and abort condition judgments, exception confirmation, collision avoidance decisions, docking and undocking manoeuvring, pilotage communication, and emergency escalation are still checked and owned by personnel holding the corresponding license or certificate of competency; even when autonomous or remote systems are used, the human control chain must remain clear.

entries.answer: The passage plan and abort conditions, exception confirmation, collision avoidance and manoeuvring decisions, docking and undocking and narrow-water manoeuvring, adoption and correction of pilot orders, signing of watch and rest and compliance records, and checking raw information against automatic alarms must all be completed and documented by an authorized person.

subject.name: Captains, Mates, and Pilots of Water Vessels
subject.summary: This page's entry corresponds to captains, mates, and pilots of water vessels (O*NET-SOC 53-5021.00): commanding or supervising the operation of ships and water vessels such as tugs and ferries, and in the United States generally requiring a license issued by the U.S. Coast Guard — directing course and speed based on local wind, weather, depth, tides, currents, and hazards, preparing passage plans from charts and navigational equipment and notices to mariners, manoeuvring vessels using radar, echo sounders, radio, and navigational aids, completing docking and undocking and narrow-water operations and the master-pilot exchange, and standing navigational watches as specified and recording voyage, watch, and compliance information; the work is mainly shipboard shifts and bridge watches (82% work more than 40 hours per week, 72% consider the consequences of errors extremely serious, 73% have extremely high responsibility for the health and safety of others), and its responsibility does not replace the owner's business decisions and the competent authority's regulation, nor does a pilot's professional duty relieve the captain and bridge watchkeeping personnel of their safety obligations.
